title: How to set up a restaurant phone system
seoTitle: Restaurant phone system setup for busy owners
description: Set up a restaurant phone system that handles calls, orders, and questions without confusion. Cover forwarding, scripts, and a simple workflow.
question: How do I set up a restaurant phone system that can take orders and handle calls without making my team miss work on the floor?
answer: Start by deciding which calls should ring the restaurant, which should forward when busy, and who will handle orders, questions, and tricky calls. Then set up forwarding with your carrier or phone system, test it from a second phone, and make sure your menu, hours, address, and order rules are easy to read for the person answering. An AI phone host like ROAL can answer calls, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and send clean tickets to the kitchen screen.
summary: You’ll be able to set up a simple restaurant phone system that answers calls, takes orders, and routes the rest to staff.
intro:
A restaurant phone system should do three things well: answer the phone fast, take accurate orders, and get tricky calls to a real person. If your current setup does not do that, it is costing you time on the line and attention on the floor.

The simplest setup is to keep your existing number, forward it when needed, and use a phone host that can handle order-taking, menu questions, and basic guest requests. ROAL is built for that kind of setup, and it can be tested in the browser before you go live.

sections.h2: What should a restaurant phone system handle first?
sections.body:
Start with the calls that matter most to your shop. For most independent restaurants, that means pickup orders, delivery orders, hours, address, parking, and menu questions. If you also take reservations or catering requests, make sure those can be captured cleanly too.

A practical way to sort this out is to list the call types your team hears every day:
- Orders for pickup or delivery
- “What time do you close?” questions
- “Where should I park?” questions
- Reservation requests
- Catering, complaints, and allergy-sensitive calls

A good phone system should keep the easy calls moving and send the unusual ones to staff with a short summary. For example, the phone host can say, “I can help with the menu and place your order now, and I’ll pass your special request to the team.” That keeps the front counter from getting buried in the same questions over and over.

sections.h2: How do I set up call forwarding without confusing customers?
sections.body:
The cleanest setup is usually to keep your restaurant’s current number and forward calls to your phone host when needed. ROAL gives each location its own phone line, then you forward your existing number to it. You can forward all calls, or only when the line is busy or unanswered.

For many landlines and some carriers, *72 followed by the forwarding number turns on forwarding, and *73 turns it off. On GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless commonly uses *72 and *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually handle forwarding in the web portal.

Use this quick checklist:
1. Confirm your carrier or phone system.
2. Set up forwarding to the new line.
3. Call your restaurant from a second phone.
4. Check that a live ring, busy ring, and unanswered ring behave the way you expect.

Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your provider and test with a real call. If you want a reference while you set it up, see [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What does a good order-taking script sound like?
sections.body:
Your phone system should make the order process simple and consistent. The caller should hear a short greeting, a clear order flow, and a final repeat-back before the order is sent to the kitchen.

A strong phone script might sound like this:
- “Thanks for calling. How can I help with your order today?”
- “What size would you like?”
- “Any modifiers or notes for that item?”
- “Can I get your name and phone number?”
- “Your ready time is about 25 minutes.”
- “Let me repeat that back before I send it in.”

ROAL does this from the restaurant’s live menu, so it can quote only the items you actually sell and avoid items marked sold out. It also speaks the caller’s language, which helps when your neighborhood gets busy and the calls come in from different types of guests. The key is to keep payment out of the phone call: it does not take card numbers over the phone, and payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it.

sections.h2: How much should a restaurant phone system cost?
sections.body:
The real question is not just what it costs per month. It is what it costs when calls come in, when the line is busy, and when someone has to stop work to answer the phone.

Here is a simple way to compare options:

| Option | Common pricing style | What to watch |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery apps | Commission per order, often around 15–30% | High order fees can add up fast |
| Human answering services | Per minute or per call | Costs can rise with longer calls |
| Monthly AI phone tools | Fixed monthly fee, often around $79–$599 per location | You may pay even in slow weeks |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed phone order | No monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee |

Use your own numbers. Say a $28 average order and 40 completed phone orders in a month. With ROAL, that would be 40 × $0.90, or $36 in order fees for that month. Compare that with your current setup and plug in your own order count, because every restaurant is different. A [phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) can help you do the math with your real numbers.

sections.h2: How do I launch without training my whole team?
sections.body:
You do not need a long software rollout to get started. A good setup should be simple enough for an owner to handle between lunch and dinner.

With ROAL, the basic flow is:
1. Paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or just your name and city at /try.
2. Let it read your menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or upload a menu in any format.
3. Test-call the host in the browser.
4. Claim the host and forward your existing number to it.
5. Decide whether calls should forward all the time or only when busy or unanswered.

You also get a kitchen screen with live tickets, call history with transcripts and recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. The owner picks the host’s voice and name, and questions the host cannot answer land in an inbox so you can answer once and the host knows it from then on. That keeps the setup practical for a small team.

sections.h2: What should I do with hard calls, complaints, and edge cases?
sections.body:
No restaurant phone system should try to fake its way through every call. Some calls belong with a person, especially allergy questions, complaints, catering, and manager requests.

Set a clear handoff rule for your staff. For example:
- Allergy-sensitive question: send to staff with a summary.
- Complaint about a missing item: send to staff with caller name and phone.
- Catering inquiry: send to staff with order size and timing.
- Reservation request: capture details and pass it along.

A simple staff note can sound like this: “Caller said no peanuts, wants to confirm if the sauce contains sesame, asked for a manager callback.” That is much better than forcing the caller through a maze. If you want more ideas for tough calls, see [complaint handoffs from your phone host](/blog/ai-host-complaint-handoff). If you are comparing options, [AI phone host vs hiring phone staff](/compare/hiring-phone-staff) can help you think through the tradeoffs. For a first test, you can [build a free test host](/try) from your website and hear how it sounds before you forward anything live.

takeaways: Keep your existing number and forward it instead of replacing it.
Make sure the phone system can take orders, answer menu questions, and pass hard calls to staff.
Use your real menu and hours so callers hear accurate answers.
Compare monthly fees, per-minute billing, and per-order pricing with your own order volume.
Test call the setup before you go live and confirm forwarding with your carrier.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant phone number to a new system?
faq.a: Most restaurants can forward their current number through the carrier, landline codes, or the business phone portal. Some common codes are *72 and *73 on many landlines, **21*number# and ##21# on some mobile carriers, and carrier-specific options for busy or unanswered calls. Always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call before relying on it.

faq.q: Can a restaurant phone system take orders from my menu?
faq.a: Yes, if the phone system is built for restaurant orders and can read your menu correctly. ROAL takes pickup and delivery orders from the restaurant’s live menu, including items, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It does not offer items marked sold out.

faq.q: Should I forward all calls or only unanswered calls?
faq.a: That depends on your staffing. If you are short on the line, forwarding all calls can keep the phone from ringing at the host stand or kitchen. If you still want staff to answer first, many owners choose busy or unanswered forwarding so the restaurant keeps control during slower moments.

faq.q: How much does a restaurant phone system usually cost?
faq.a: Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, even if order volume is light. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call, while delivery apps commonly take a commission per order. ROAL uses per-completed-order pricing at $0.90, with no monthly fee, setup fee, per-minute fee, or contract.
